senses: A papal decree, particularly one derived from an ecclesiastical letter.
ety: From Middle French decretal, from Late Latin dēcrētālis, from Latin decretum.

ety: From Latin priapismus, from Priapus (“the god of procreation, the penis”) + -ism, from Ancient Greek πριαπισμός (priapismós).

That which lengthens out; a continuation.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin elongatio, elongationem.

senses: A rheostat that is used to vary the intensity of a domestic electric light
A switch used to select between the low and high headlamp beam on a road vehicle. (usually as "dimmer switch", primarily in North America; elsewhere "dipswitch" or "dipper switch")
Chef's choice.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese お任(まか)せ (omakase, “it's up to you”).
examples: So Americans are stuck between chef-driven omakase meals at elite restaurants that cost a fortune and the cheap, predictable fare at our neighborhood places.
He prefers a greasy cheeseburger to a hundred-dollar omakase sushi dinner.
An omakase menu is available, as are sushi plates, which consist of a variety of nigiri, maki, and/or sashimi chosen by the chef.

senses: One who wakens or arouses from sleep.
One who wakes somebody or something.
An alarm clock.
ety: From Middle English wakere, equivalent to wake + -er. Compare West Frisian wekker (“alarm clock”, literally “waker”), Dutch wekker, German Wecker.

senses: Something or someone who makes a sound.
An instrument used in telegraphy in place of a register, the communications being read by sound.
Synonym of sting (“brief musical sequence in television etc.”).
ety: From Middle English soundar, sownere, equivalent to sound + -er.

senses: A representation of hierarchical data as a set of nested rectangles.
That which zooms.
A kind of small swim fin.
A baby boomer with a very active lifestyle.
An eccentric, erratic or crazy person, particularly associated with more extreme supporters of Scottish nationalism.
ety: From zoom + -er. The sense of "active baby boomer" is influenced by the word boomer, and is attributed to Moses Znaimer.
examples: A recent study released by the Conference Board of Canada states that the Zoomers (Baby Boomers who refuse to age), Gen X and Gen Y have more in common than we might think.

ety: From Das + -tinib, after its discoverer, the chemist Jagabandhu Das.
examples: In 2009, Mayfield still remains in remission, now on dasatinib.

senses: Adventurous; venturesome; willing to undertake activities involving risk.
Of, related to or produced by a synod; synodal.
ety: From Latin synodicus, from Ancient Greek συνοδικός (sunodikós, “of or related to an assembly or meeting”). Equivalent to synod + -ic.

senses: A dark purple colour, like that of some petunia flowers.
ety: Borrowed from taxonomic name Petunia, from (now obsolete) French pétun (“tobacco”), from Old Tupi petyma (“tobacco”).

senses: A person who erects and dismantles scaffolding.

senses: A person who provokes or takes part in an insurrection.
examples: It comes from the Latin insurgo, meaning “to rise up within”: so insurrectionists are, etymologically, the same as “insurgents”, even if that is normally a word for those who do not meekly accept western military rule.

senses: Someone interested in words; especially, one enthusiastic about the study of word use but not bent on being pedantic about usage prescription.
ety: From word + -ie; the enthusiast sense is parallel in nature with foodie and was probably influenced by it.

senses: A purplish-red colour.

senses: A female wonk.
Tenderness, gentle intimacy or affection.

senses: of the repulsion of atoms due to closeness or arrangement
Characteristic of what is considered the ideal behaviour pertaining to fatherhood.
Befitting of a father; protective, paternal.
ety: From Middle English faderly, from Old English fæderlīċ (“fatherly, paternal”), from Proto-West Germanic *faderlīk, from Proto-Germanic *fadurlīkaz (“fatherly, paternal”), equivalent to father + -ly. Cognate with West Frisian faderlik (“fatherly”), Dutch vaderlijk (“fatherly”), German väterlich (“fatherly”), Danish faderlig (“fatherly”), Swedish faderlig (“fatherly”), Icelandic föðurlegur (“fatherly”) . Doublet of fatherlike.

senses: A spelling, word, or phrase used in common speech that is considered improper or incorrect for formal communication.
examples: We never descended to the vulgarism of a quarrel. People said that neither of us had a heart, but it appears to me that politeness is an excellent substitute.
Editors of newspapers allow more vulgarisms to go to print today than they used to.

senses: Of the metatarsus.
Covered in pills (particles created by mechanical wear).
Characterized by or involving many pills.
ety: From pill + -y. In some cases, pill is a clipping of a longer word.
examples: After many washings, my favorite sweater is faded and pilly.
I gave the superintendent a deposit and I got a room on the third floor with a bed that had sheets and a pilly blanket and a pillow so flat you had to fold it over to rest your head on it.
One was a young woman with stringy brown hair, a pilly black sweater and fabulous boots of parti-coloured suede.

senses: Turning to stone: the process of replacement of the organic residues of plants (and animals) with insoluble salts, with the original shape and topography being retained.
obduracy; callousness.

ety: From French pétrification, from Middle French pétrifier + -ation.

senses: The property of being modular.

ety: Blend of mathematics + athlete. The term is a registered trademark of the MathCounts organization. The term entered pop culture from the movies American Pie (1999) and Mean Girls (2004), as well as being featured in the short-lived cult TV series Freaks and Geeks. Mathletes was the name of a US national organization in the 1970s that sponsored high school mathematics competitions ("Mathletes") and junior high school competitions ("Junior Mathletes") between school teams known as "Math Teams".
